newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Powerless Australian dlr mauled in US$/yen mayhem.
newsitem.headline: Powerless Australian dlr mauled in US$/yen mayhem.

text.p: The Australian dollar clung tightly to its U.S. counterpart Tuesday as both were buried beneath a torrent of distressed selling against the yen.

The U.S. currency was stripped of 2-1/2 yen to hit a 1997 low on a corrosive mix of speculation the Federal Reserve would not tighten at its policy meeting today but Japan would soon be raising rates. At least that was the rationale, although traders suspected it had more to do with herd instinct today.
"This is a stampede, pure and simple," said one, complaining of foot prints down his spine and across his profit and loss book. "It's man the life boats, women and spot traders first."
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the dollar had collapsed to 87.10/20 yen, its lowest local close since late September, from 89.42/52 at the opening and 89.94/04 late here Monday.
The slump brought its losses to a spectacular 13 percent since the currency peaked just above 100.00 on May 1.
In contrast trading was positively comatose against the U.S. dollar where the A$ held to a tight US$0.7725/7750 range for the entire session to end at US$0.7741/46 from US$0.7745/50 Monday.
Dealers said US$0.7720 proved solid as it had for six weeks but, worringly for bulls, there was talk a big Asian buyer had withdrawn when an option position he was protecting expired.

But all that was just a sideshow to the main event as US$/yen plunged to 112.50 yen from an early 115.65 -- a 2.7 percent drop in 12 hours. And dealers saw more pain ahead unless the Federal Reserve hiked U.S. rates at its meeting tonight.
Once upon a time the market had been confident the Fed would tighten today, but low U.S. inflation and a slowing in some key growth indicators turned that to utter uncertainty.
Whatever the decision it would have conflicting implications for the A$, making it hard to gauge the near term reaction.
For one thing a hike should help US$/yen bounce, which in turn would tend to drag the dollar bloc higher on the crosses.
But it would also narrow the local dollar's interest differential over the U.S. unit to just 25 basis points, making it less attractive on a pure yield basis.
Some argued a U.S. hike would ultimately benefit the A$ by making a domestic rate cut less likely.
A 0.25 point Fed rise meant a 0.5 point cut here would take domestic rates below those in the U.S. for the first time since the early 1980's when the exchange rate was fixed.
Analysts were unsure how offshore investors would react now the currency was floating so freely, but suspected the A$ could take a beating while they got used to the novelty.
Some felt the RBA would be reluctant to risk such a slide given that the strength of the dollar had played a major part in bringing Australian inflation back into its target range.

But if the Fed stayed silent it might equally be seen as a window of opportunity for the RBA to get in one more easing. Analysts said it was clear from all the political rhetoric after last week's 1997/98 budget that the government was looking for the RBA to cut again.
Indeed, there were rumours the Treasury had asked for an easing at the last RBA board meeting but the bank declined because of rising wages growth.
Treasury was thought to have argued, as do some economists, aggregate wages data overstate the danger and key figures this week will show private sector wage deals were resonably subdued.

The Department of Industrial Relations releases its estimate of enterprise bargain deals for the March quarter on Wednesday. The December quarter report showed wage growth in the private sector slowed to 4.4 percent from 5.3 percent in Q3, and for all sectors to 4.4 percent from 4.8 percent.
Some were counting on a further slowdown, although a survey by HSBC Markets on Monday suggested the pace of wage deals may have actually picked up a touch in Q1.
More important will be the final figures on Q1 average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) which are due Thursday.
The initial data showed a surprisingly strong rise in wages to an annual 4.6 percent from 3.9 percent in Q3, a jump which the RBA called a setback for the inflation outlook.

But there was an argument it had been biased upwards by special circumstances in the public sector and the detailed breakdown would show private wage deals were running in the region of 3.0 to 3.5 percent. Since these were what mattered for inflation, such a result would revive speculation of another rate cut. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
